blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 17)
In the previous part, we explored how to estimate memory for an LLM inference workload.
The basic equation was:

Total memory
=
model weights
+
KV cache
+
runtime overhead
But the deeper lesson was:

Weights determine whether the model can load.

KV cache determines how much workload
the system can serve.
We also saw that memory requirements grow with:

context length
concurrent requests
batch size
generated tokens
That naturally leads to the next question:

What happens when one inference server
is no longer enough?
We can create more replicas.
We can add more GPUs.
We can deploy the model across a Kubernetes cluster.
But once we do that, another set of problems appears:

Which replica should receive each request?

Where is the request's KV cache?

Which replica has enough memory?

Which replica has the shortest queue?

Should prefill and decode run together?

How should the system scale?
This is where llm-d becomes interesting.
This article continues directly from the memory-planning questions in Part 16.
What is llm-d?
At a high level:

llm-d
=
a distributed inference serving stack
It helps coordinate LLM inference across multiple model servers, accelerators, nodes, and replicas.
A model server such as vLLM or SGLang runs the actual model.
llm-d sits around those model servers and helps coordinate them as one distributed serving system.
A simple mental model is:

vLLM / SGLang
=
runs the model efficiently

llm-d
=
coordinates many model servers efficiently

The project’s primary architecture is Kubernetes-native. Its official documentation describes llm-d as a composable stack that coordinates model-server pods using LLM-aware routing, distributed KV-cache management, disaggregated serving, multi-node execution, and autoscaling. It supports multiple inference engines and accelerator platforms. (llm-d)
Is llm-d an inference engine like vLLM?
No.
This distinction is very important.
vLLM is an inference engine.
It handles things like:

model execution
continuous batching
PagedAttention
KV cache allocation
prefill
decode
token sampling
llm-d operates at a higher level.
It handles things like:

routing between model servers
cluster-level request scheduling
KV-cache locality across replicas
prefill/decode disaggregation
flow control
autoscaling
multi-node deployment patterns
So the architecture may look like:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
vLLM Model Server
  ↓
GPU Workers
  ↓
Model Computation
llm-d does not replace vLLM.
It coordinates a fleet of engines such as vLLM or SGLang.
What problem does llm-d solve?
Suppose we deploy three replicas of the same model:

Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
Each replica may have:

its own scheduler
its own KV cache
its own request queue
its own GPU memory
its own active batches
Now requests start arriving.
A traditional load balancer may distribute them without understanding the internal state of each inference replica.
For example:

Request A → Replica 1
Request B → Replica 2
Request C → Replica 3
Request D → Replica 1
That may work for normal web applications.
But LLM requests are not normal web requests.
The best destination may depend on:

which replica already has the prompt prefix cached
which replica has free KV-cache capacity
which replica has the shortest queue
which replica can meet the latency target
which replica is a prefill worker
which replica is a decode worker
A generic load balancer usually does not understand these details.
llm-d introduces an inference-aware routing and scheduling layer.
Why is normal load balancing not enough?
Imagine two model replicas:

Replica 1 → 40% GPU utilization
Replica 2 → 40% GPU utilization
At first glance, both look equally healthy.
But internally:

Replica 1:
- has the request's prefix cached
- has enough free KV blocks
- has a short decode queue

Replica 2:
- does not have the prefix cached
- has high KV-cache pressure
- has several long prompts waiting
A normal load balancer might see:

Replica 1 = healthy
Replica 2 = healthy
An inference-aware router sees:
Replica 1 is probably a much better destination.
That difference can affect:

time to first token
queueing time
prefill work
KV-cache hit rate
GPU utilization
total throughputIs llm-d only a smarter load balancer?
No.
Intelligent routing is one of its central capabilities, but llm-d covers a larger distributed inference problem.
A useful mental model is:

Load balancer
=
send traffic across endpoints

llm-d
=
understand inference state
and coordinate traffic, memory,
workers, phases, and scaling
Its major capabilities include:

LLM-aware routing
KV-cache-aware scheduling
distributed KV-cache indexing
KV-cache offloading
prefill/decode disaggregation
flow control
autoscaling
multi-node serving patterns
benchmarking and deployment recipes
The stack is composable, so operators can adopt only the pieces they need rather than deploying every capability at once. (GitHub)
What are the main parts of llm-d?
The current architecture is organized around three core concepts:

Router
InferencePool
Model Server
The official architecture describes them as follows:

Router
=
the intelligent entry point

InferencePool
=
the group of eligible model servers

Model Server
=
the engine that executes the model
(GitHub)
What is the llm-d Router?
The Router receives inference traffic and decides where it should go.
It has two major functional parts:

Proxy
+
Endpoint Picker
The proxy handles the actual network request.
The Endpoint Picker, usually called the EPP, provides the routing intelligence.
The flow looks like:

Request
  ↓
Proxy
  ↓
Endpoint Picker
  ↓
Selected Model Server
The proxy may be an L7 proxy such as Envoy.
The Endpoint Picker examines the eligible model servers and scores them.
It then tells the proxy which endpoint should receive the request.
What does the Endpoint Picker consider?
The Endpoint Picker can consider signals such as:

prefix-cache locality
KV-cache utilization
queue depth
session affinity
model metadata
configured routing policies
So it is not simply asking:
Which replica is next?
It is asking:

Which replica is currently
the best destination for this request?
The official llm-d documentation identifies prefix-cache locality, available KV-cache capacity, and queue depth as core scoring signals. (GitHub)
What is an InferencePool?
An InferencePool groups model-server endpoints that can serve the same base model.
Imagine:

InferencePool: Qwen-Model

├── Model Server A
├── Model Server B
├── Model Server C
└── Model Server D
The Router does not need to manually track every server.
It discovers the eligible servers through the InferencePool.
A useful mental model is:

Kubernetes Service
=
generic group of application endpoints

InferencePool
=
LLM-aware group of model-server endpoints
The InferencePool becomes the Router’s discovery target.
What is an InferencePool variant?
Not every server inside an InferencePool must have the same role.
Some servers may be optimized for:
prefill
Others may be optimized for:
decode
Some may use:

different hardware
different cost profiles
different latency profiles
different throughput profiles
llm-d represents these logical subgroups using labels called variants.
For example:

InferencePool: Model-X

Prefill Variant:
├── Prefill Server 1
└── Prefill Server 2

Decode Variant:
├── Decode Server 1
├── Decode Server 2
└── Decode Server 3
The Router can then choose endpoints based on the role needed for that request.
What is a Model Server?
The Model Server is the component that actually executes the model.
Examples include:

vLLM
SGLang
The Model Server handles the local inference work:

tokenization
prefill
decode
KV-cache operations
continuous batching
model execution
token generation
The Model Server may use:

one GPU
multiple GPUs
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
multi-node workers
From llm-d’s perspective, it is an endpoint capable of performing a particular inference role.
What does a basic llm-d architecture look like?
At a high level:

Client
  ↓
Gateway / Proxy
  ↓
Endpoint Picker
  ↓
InferencePool
  ├── Model Server A
  ├── Model Server B
  ├── Model Server C
  └── Model Server D
Or more simply:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Best Model Server
  ↓
Inference Engine
  ↓
Accelerators
What happens when a request arrives?
Suppose the user sends:
"Explain distributed inference"
The flow may look like this:

1. Request reaches the gateway.

2. Proxy asks the Endpoint Picker
   where the request should go.

3. Endpoint Picker examines
   the available model servers.

4. It considers:
   - queue depth
   - cache locality
   - KV-cache pressure
   - server role
   - routing policy

5. It selects a model server.

6. Proxy forwards the request.

7. The model server performs
   prefill and decode.

8. Generated tokens stream
   back to the user.
The important point is:

The routing decision is aware
of LLM inference state.
How is the llm-d Router different from the vLLM scheduler?
This is another important distinction.
The llm-d Router decides:
Which model server should receive the request?
The vLLM scheduler decides:

Which requests inside this model server
should run during the next engine step?
So:

llm-d Router
=
cluster-level scheduling

vLLM Scheduler
=
engine-level scheduling
The full flow is:

Incoming Request
  ↓
llm-d chooses a model server
  ↓
vLLM admits the request
  ↓
vLLM places it into prefill/decode batches
  ↓
GPU executes the work
Both schedulers matter.
They simply operate at different levels.
How is this different from model routing?
Earlier in the series, we discussed model routing.
A model router may decide:

Simple request → small CPU model

Complex request → large GPU model

Document request → document model
That answers:
Which model or service should handle this request?
llm-d usually answers a different question:

Which serving endpoint for the selected model
should handle this request?
So:

Model Router
=
choose the model or service

llm-d Router
=
choose the best inference endpoint
inside the distributed serving system
A complete platform may use both:

User
  ↓
Model Router
  ↓
Large Model Service selected
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Best model-server endpoint
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
GPU
Why is KV-cache-aware routing important?
Suppose every request begins with the same large system prompt:

"You are an enterprise support assistant.
Follow these policies...
Use these product documents..."
That shared prefix may contain thousands of tokens.
Replica 1 has already processed that prefix.
Its KV cache contains the corresponding blocks.
Now another request arrives with the same prefix.
The Router has two choices.
Choice 1
Send the request to Replica 2:

Replica 2 has no cached prefix.

It must recompute the full prefill.
Choice 2
Send it to Replica 1:

Replica 1 already has the prefix cached.

It can reuse the cached computation.
Choice 2 may avoid a large amount of repeated prefill work.
That can improve:

TTFT
throughput
GPU efficiency
cost per request
What does normal round-robin routing do here?
A simple routing policy may produce:

Request 1 → Replica A
Request 2 → Replica B
Request 3 → Replica C
Request 4 → Replica A
Even when all four requests share the same prefix.
The cache becomes scattered.
Each replica may repeatedly process the same tokens.
The cluster has more hardware, but it is still wasting computation.
KV-cache-aware routing tries to preserve locality:

Requests with reusable prefixes
→ replicas containing those prefixes
llm-d supports prefix-cache-aware routing and can maintain an index of which token blocks are present on which model servers. (GitHub)
Is prefix-cache-aware routing the same as a sticky session?
Not exactly.
A sticky session usually means:

Same user
→ same replica
Prefix-cache-aware routing means:

Request
→ replica containing the most useful prefix
Sometimes these result in the same choice.
But not always.
For example, many different users may share:

the same system prompt
the same document prefix
the same agent instructions
the same cached conversation history
Prefix-aware routing can potentially reuse that shared state even when the users are different.
So the routing decision is based on:
cache similarity
not only:
user identity
What does distributed KV cache mean?
It does not necessarily mean there is one giant shared GPU memory space.
Instead, it usually means:

KV-cache blocks are distributed
across multiple model servers.
For example:

Replica A:
Prefix X blocks

Replica B:
Prefix Y blocks

Replica C:
Prefix Z blocks
The distributed serving system needs to know:

which blocks exist
where they exist
whether they can be reused
whether they should be transferred
whether they should be offloaded
So a better mental model is:

Distributed KV cache
=
many local caches
+
cluster-level knowledge
+
routing and transfer mechanisms
What is KV-cache indexing?
KV-cache indexing means maintaining information about where cached token blocks live.
Imagine a logical index:

Prefix A → Replica 1
Prefix B → Replica 3
Prefix C → Replica 1 and Replica 2
When a request arrives, the Router can consult this information.
It may discover:

Replica 1 has 80% of the prefix cached.

Replica 2 has 20% cached.

Replica 3 has none.
But cache locality is not the only factor.
Perhaps Replica 1 is overloaded.
Then the Router must balance:

reuse cached computation
vs
avoid an overloaded replica
That is what makes inference routing a real scheduling problem.
Does the Router always choose the replica with the largest cache hit?
Not necessarily.
Suppose:

Replica 1:
90% prefix match
very long queue

Replica 2:
70% prefix match
almost idle
The best choice may depend on:

estimated prefill cost
queue waiting time
KV-cache capacity
latency target
request priority
So an intelligent policy may calculate something like:

Expected completion time
=
queue delay
+
missing prefill work
+
decode time
The best destination is not always the emptiest replica.
It is also not always the replica with the highest cache match.
The router must consider both.
How does this connect to memory planning?
In Part 16, we used:

Total memory
=
weights
+
KV cache
+
overhead
That formula still applies to every model server.
llm-d does not make the memory requirement disappear.
Instead, it helps coordinate memory across the fleet.
For example:

Replica A is low on KV space.

Replica B has more free blocks.

Replica C contains a valuable cached prefix.
The Router can consider that information when selecting a destination.
So the memory question becomes:

Not only:
Does the cluster have enough memory?

But also:
Where is that memory available?
Where is useful state already cached?
Does llm-d make model weights smaller?
No.
llm-d does not quantize the model.
It does not reduce the parameter count.
It does not replace tensor parallelism.
If a model needs 80 GB of weight memory, the model still needs approximately that memory somewhere in the serving topology.
llm-d helps coordinate:

where model servers run
how requests reach them
how KV cache is reused
how workers are scaled
how runtime phases are distributed
It improves orchestration.
It does not change the mathematical size of the model.
What is KV-cache offloading?
GPU memory is fast, but limited.
Once GPU HBM becomes full, the system may need another place to store less-active KV-cache blocks.
A memory hierarchy may look like:

GPU HBM
  ↓
CPU memory
  ↓
local or shared storage
The fastest and most active blocks remain close to the accelerator.
Other blocks may be moved to a slower, larger tier.
When those blocks are needed again, they can be restored.
A useful analogy is:

GPU KV cache
=
hot working set

CPU memory
=
warm cache tier

Storage
=
larger cold cache tier
llm-d supports KV-cache management patterns that include cache indexing and tiered offloading beyond accelerator memory. (GitHub)
Does offloading make memory unlimited?
No.
Offloading expands effective capacity, but slower tiers have costs.
Moving data between:

GPU
CPU
storage
takes time and bandwidth.
So the tradeoff becomes:

recompute the prefix
vs
reload cached KV blocks
If loading the cache is faster than recomputing it, reuse may help.
If the cache is stored too far away or the network is slow, recomputation may be cheaper.
Again, the correct decision depends on the workload and infrastructure.
What is prefill/decode disaggregation?
Earlier, we learned that inference has two different runtime phases:

Prefill
and
Decode
Prefill processes the prompt.
Decode generates tokens one at a time.
These phases have different performance characteristics.
A simple model server handles both:

Model Server
├── Prefill
└── Decode
This is called a monolithic deployment.
Prefill/decode disaggregation separates them:

Prefill Workers
+
Decode Workers
Now one set of workers processes prompts.
Another set generates output tokens.
How is this different from tensor or pipeline parallelism?
The distinction is:

Tensor Parallelism
=
split tensors inside a layer

Pipeline Parallelism
=
split model layers

Data Parallelism
=
replicate the model-serving unit

Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
=
split runtime phases
With prefill/decode disaggregation:

Prefill cluster
=
optimized for prompt processing

Decode cluster
=
optimized for token generation
Each cluster may still use:

tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
data parallelism
So disaggregation does not replace the earlier parallelism strategies.
It exists at another layer.
What does a disaggregated request flow look like?
Suppose a user sends a long prompt.
The flow may be:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
Prefill Worker
  ↓
Prompt is processed
  ↓
KV cache is created
  ↓
KV cache is transferred
  ↓
Decode Worker
  ↓
Tokens are generated
  ↓
Response streams to user
The Router must therefore choose two destinations:

Which prefill worker?

Which decode worker?
It must also coordinate the handoff between them.
Why separate prefill and decode?
Because they stress hardware differently.
Prefill usually involves:

many input tokens
large matrix operations
high compute utilization
Decode usually involves:

one token per sequence per step
repeated weight and KV-cache reads
latency-sensitive execution
memory-bandwidth pressure
When both phases share the same workers, large prefill requests can interfere with active decode requests.
For example:

Long prompt arrives
  ↓
Large prefill starts
  ↓
Existing decode requests slow down
  ↓
Inter-token latency increases
By separating the phases, operators can scale and tune them independently.
What does independent scaling mean?
Suppose the workload has very long prompts but short outputs.
The system may need:

more prefill capacity
fewer decode workers
Another workload may have short prompts but very long responses.
It may need:

fewer prefill workers
more decode capacity
With a monolithic deployment, each replica contains both capabilities.
With disaggregation, the ratio can be adjusted:

2 Prefill Workers
+
6 Decode Workers
or:

6 Prefill Workers
+
2 Decode Workers
That can better match the workload shape.
What is the major cost of disaggregation?
The KV cache must move from the prefill worker to the decode worker.
That transfer can be large.
The request cannot begin decode until the required KV-cache state is available.
So networking becomes part of the critical path.
The flow is now:

Prefill compute
+
KV-cache transfer
+
Decode compute
A slow transfer directly increases time to first token.

Current llm-d disaggregated serving uses transfer mechanisms such as NIXL with high-speed network transports. The project’s networking guidance emphasizes that KV-cache transfer time becomes a first-order contributor to TTFT. (GitHub)
Does prefill/decode disaggregation always improve performance?
No.
It depends on:

prompt length
output length
request concurrency
GPU topology
network bandwidth
transfer latency
prefill/decode worker ratio
For a small model with short prompts, the transfer overhead may not be worthwhile.
For long-context workloads where prefill heavily interferes with decode, separation may be useful.
So disaggregation should not be treated as:
always faster
It should be treated as:

a topology that may improve performance
for the right workload

Official llm-d benchmarks have also shown that the benefit varies with concurrency and workload shape, which is why the project provides tested configurations rather than presenting one universal topology. (llm-d)
What are llm-d’s “well-lit paths”?
Distributed inference has many possible configurations.
For example:

How many prefill workers?
How many decode workers?
Which tensor-parallel size?
Which networking backend?
Which cache policy?
Which routing policy?
Which autoscaling metric?
There is no single answer that works everywhere.
llm-d uses the term:
Well-Lit Paths
for tested and benchmarked deployment recipes.
A well-lit path may include:

deployment manifests
Helm configurations
hardware assumptions
performance settings
sample workloads
benchmark results
observability configuration
The idea is:

Do not start with an empty page.

Start with a tested pattern,
measure it,
then adapt it.
The project documents well-lit paths for patterns such as intelligent scheduling, disaggregated serving, and large multi-node workloads. (GitHub)
How does flow control fit into llm-d?
Suppose every model server maintains its own isolated queue.
The Router sends a request to Replica A.
Immediately afterward, Replica A becomes overloaded.
The request is now stuck behind work already assigned to that server.
Another replica may become free, but the request has already been committed.
Flow control can delay the final endpoint decision until capacity is available.
This is sometimes called:
late-binding scheduling
Instead of:

Request arrives
→ immediately assign replica
→ wait in that replica's queue
the system can use:

Request arrives
→ hold in an inference-aware queue
→ choose the best replica
  when capacity becomes available
This gives the Router more current information when making the decision.
Why is centralized queueing useful?
It can help prevent this situation:

Replica A:
10 requests waiting

Replica B:
0 requests waiting
while another new request is accidentally sent to Replica A.
A cluster-level queue gives the routing system a better view of total demand.
It can also support:

request priorities
tenant fairness
interactive vs batch traffic
admission control
latency SLOs
Current llm-d routing capabilities include policy-aware flow control, priority dispatch, late binding, and guardrails for requests that cannot meet configured latency objectives. (GitHub)
What is admission control?
Admission control asks:
Should this request enter the serving system now?
Suppose every replica is saturated.
The system has several choices:

accept the request and let latency explode

queue the request

reject the request

send it to another model or cluster
Sometimes accepting everything is worse than rejecting some traffic.
If the system keeps admitting requests beyond capacity:

queues grow
KV-cache pressure grows
TTFT increases
inter-token latency increases
timeouts increase
Admission control protects the requests already being served.
How does autoscaling fit into this?
Kubernetes can add or remove model-server replicas.
But traditional autoscaling often looks at:

CPU utilization
GPU utilization
Those signals alone may not describe inference demand well.
A GPU can be highly utilized but still healthy.
Another GPU can look underutilized while its KV cache is almost full.
More useful inference signals may include:

queue depth
request arrival rate
active sequences
KV-cache pressure
TTFT
TPOT
throughput
pending token work
llm-d can expose router-level demand metrics for Kubernetes autoscaling and also supports more advanced workload-variant scaling patterns. (GitHub)
What is a workload variant?
Suppose the same model is available in several forms:

Variant A:
expensive GPU
low latency

Variant B:
cheaper GPU
higher throughput

Variant C:
quantized model
lower cost
Or:

Variant A:
prefill workers

Variant B:
decode workers
Variants allow the platform to distinguish these serving profiles.
An autoscaler or router can then reason about:

which variant should grow
which variant should shrink
which variant can meet the SLO
which variant is most cost-effective
Does llm-d replace Kubernetes?
No.
llm-d builds on Kubernetes.
Kubernetes still manages:

pods
nodes
deployments
networking
health checks
resource requests
scheduling
restarts
scaling primitives
llm-d adds inference-specific intelligence.
A simple mental model is:

Kubernetes
=
manages workloads and infrastructure

llm-d
=
manages distributed inference behavior
Is llm-d limited to Kubernetes?
llm-d was designed as a Kubernetes-native project, and its main architecture uses resources such as Gateways, InferencePools, labels, Deployments, and autoscaling primitives.

However, the project has also introduced a discovery mode that lets its routing intelligence operate outside Kubernetes environments. The central routing ideas—KV-cache awareness, prefix affinity, flow control, and disaggregated routing—do not fundamentally require Kubernetes. (llm-d)
For this series, the most useful starting point is still:

llm-d
=
Kubernetes-native distributed inference
because that is where the architecture is easiest to connect with LLMOps.
Does llm-d only work with vLLM?
No.
vLLM has been a major engine in the llm-d ecosystem, but the architecture is designed to support multiple model servers.
Current project documentation lists engines such as:

vLLM
SGLang
and multiple accelerator platforms. (GitHub)
The key abstraction is:
Model Server
As long as the server exposes the interfaces and signals required by the stack, it can participate in the distributed serving architecture.
Does llm-d make a single request faster?
Not automatically.
If there is:

one model server
one request
no reusable prefix
no queue
no memory pressure
adding a distributed routing layer may not help much.
The main benefits appear when the system has:

multiple replicas
many concurrent requests
repeated prefixes
long prompts
KV-cache pressure
different worker roles
strict latency targets
llm-d is primarily about improving system-level behavior.
It tries to make the whole fleet more efficient.
When might llm-d be unnecessary?
A simple deployment may not need it.
For example:

one local model
one vLLM server
small traffic
no Kubernetes
no scaling requirement
In that case:

Application
  ↓
vLLM
  ↓
GPU
may be enough.
Adding llm-d would introduce:

more components
more configuration
more observability needs
more networking complexity
Distributed systems should solve an actual scaling problem.
They should not be added only because they look advanced.
When does llm-d start becoming useful?
It becomes more relevant when we have:

multiple inference replicas
large or variable workloads
long-context requests
repeated prompt prefixes
many concurrent users
prefill/decode interference
multi-node model deployments
cost or latency SLOs
Kubernetes-based operations
At that point, the problem changes from:
How do I run this model?
to:

How do I operate a fleet
of model-serving systems efficiently?
That is the problem llm-d is designed around.
What does llm-d not solve?
llm-d does not remove the fundamental limits of inference.
It does not eliminate:

autoregressive decoding
model weight memory
KV-cache growth
network latency
GPU saturation
hardware failures
It helps coordinate these constraints.
But operators still need to understand:

workload shape
capacity
memory
network topology
latency targets
cost constraints
There is no distributed system that makes these tradeoffs disappear.
What should we monitor in an llm-d deployment?
At the request level:

TTFT
TPOT / inter-token latency
end-to-end latency
request failures
queueing time
At the inference level:

input tokens/sec
output tokens/sec
active sequences
batch occupancy
prefix-cache hit rate
KV-cache utilization
At the routing level:

requests per endpoint
routing decisions
queue depth
cache-affinity score
request priority
admission failures
At the infrastructure level:

GPU utilization
GPU memory
network throughput
KV-transfer time
pod health
node health
replica count
For disaggregated serving, this metric becomes especially important:
KV-cache transfer time
Because a slow transfer directly affects the time before decode can begin.
What is the full mental model now?
The complete architecture can look like:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Model Router
  ↓
Selected Model Service
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
InferencePool
  ├── Prefill Variant
  │     ├── Prefill Worker A
  │     └── Prefill Worker B
  │
  └── Decode Variant
        ├── Decode Worker A
        ├── Decode Worker B
        └── Decode Worker C
              ↓
         vLLM / SGLang
              ↓
         GPU Workers
For a normal monolithic deployment:

User
  ↓
llm-d Router
  ↓
InferencePool

The Router chooses the best replica.
The engine scheduler manages work inside that replica.

Or:

The accelerator performs the math.
What is the biggest mental shift?
Until now, many of the articles focused on one model-serving system.
We asked:

How does one server manage KV cache?

How does one engine batch requests?

How much memory does one workload need?
llm-d moves the mental model to the cluster level.
Now the questions become:

Where is the useful cache?

Which endpoint has capacity?

Where should prefill run?

Where should decode run?

Should the KV cache move?

Should another replica start?

Can this request meet its latency target?
That is a major shift.
We are no longer only optimizing model execution.
We are optimizing:

placement
routing
memory locality
network transfers
worker specialization
cluster capacity
What is the key intuition?
The easiest summary is:

vLLM makes an inference engine efficient.

llm-d makes a fleet of inference engines
work together intelligently.
A slightly deeper version is:

llm-d connects:

Kubernetes
+
inference-aware routing
+
distributed KV-cache management
+
prefill/decode disaggregation
+
autoscaling
+
model-serving engines
Its goal is not only to add more servers.
Its goal is to use those servers more intelligently.
